nodes.text: THE MYSTICAL EXPOSITION OF BISHOP SALONIUS ON THE PARABLES OF SOLOMON.
SPEAKERS
VERANUS AND SALONIUS.
VERANUS. In what language is the word 'parables' used?
SALONIUS. In Greek; in Latin it is rendered 'likenesses'.
VERANUS. Why did Solomon give this book that name?
SALONIUS. To show by it that we ought to understand what he says not according to the letter, but otherwise and spiritually.
VERANUS. Whom does Solomon signify, in that he spoke in parables?
SALONIUS. The Lord Jesus Christ, because he spoke in parables to the crowds of the Jews; and indeed by his very name he signifies the same Lord Jesus Christ.
VERANUS. How then is 'Solomon' interpreted?

SALONIUS. 'Peaceful', or 'lovable'. It signifies him of whom the Apostle says: Christ is our peace, who has made both one (Eph. 2:14). And again: Making peace through his blood, whether the things that are in heaven or those that are on earth (Col. 1). Again, since Solomon is interpreted 'lovable', it most fittingly signifies him to whom the Father speaks, saying: You are my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased (Matt. 3).
VERANUS. What does the very peaceful state of his kingdom signify?
SALONIUS. The everlasting kingdom of Christ and of the Church, of which it is written: And of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1).
VERANUS. Why, according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters, are these sayings of Solomon called not 'parables' but 'proverbs'?

SALONIUS. Just as they are called parables because they are hidden and signify secret mysteries, so they are also fittingly called proverbs, because they are such as ought very often to be on the lips of the faithful, and to be committed to memory and retained.
VERANUS. What benefit do the parables of Solomon bestow?
SALONIUS. Wisdom, namely, and discipline; and this is what he says: For learning wisdom and discipline (Prov. 1).
VERANUS. What difference is there between wisdom and discipline?
SALONIUS. Wisdom is the knowledge of divine things, while discipline is the conduct of a holy and pure life.
VERANUS. What, then, is it to learn wisdom?
SALONIUS. To know and understand how you ought to believe rightly.
VERANUS. What is it to learn discipline?

SALONIUS. To recognise how each person ought to live, what it is fitting to do in action, and where he ought to direct the intention of his heart. There follows: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
VERANUS. How many fears of the Lord are there?
SALONIUS. Two, that is, servile and holy.
VERANUS. Why is it called servile?
SALONIUS. Because, like slaves, we serve the Lord out of fear of Gehenna, lest we be led to torments.
VERANUS. Why is it called holy fear?
SALONIUS. Because, just as a good son fears to offend the eyes of a most loving father even in a small matter, so too those who are perfect in the Church fear to offend the eyes of God by sinning.
VERANUS. Which of those two is wiser?
SALONIUS. The servile, because whoever begins to be wise, that is, recognises after his sins that he has gone astray, is first seized by divine fear, lest he be dragged to torments.
VERANUS. And what does holy fear accomplish?
SALONIUS. It increases wisdom, since perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4), that servile [fear]; but holy fear endures for ever and ever (Ps. 18).
VERANUS. What is it that Solomon says: In vain is the net cast before the eyes of the winged (Prov. 1)? Are birds not often caught in nets?
SALONIUS. They are indeed.
VERANUS. Who, then, are these winged ones?

SALONIUS. Holy and chosen men, who have the wings of faith, hope and love, and of the other virtues, by which they fly up to contemplate heavenly things; they also have spiritual eyes, with which they both foresee the snares of the ancient enemy and guard against sins. In vain, then, that is, to no purpose, is the net cast before the eyes of the winged; that is, the noose of the devil's snares is set against holy and chosen men, because those whose way of life is in heaven can easily overcome the snares of the devil on earth.
VERANUS. What is the wisdom of which Solomon says: Wisdom preaches outside, she has uttered her voice in the streets?
SALONIUS. [The wisdom] of Christ Jesus, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, as the Apostle says.
VERANUS. How, then, does this wisdom preach outside?

SALONIUS. He preached inside, that is, in secret, before he suffered, because he showed the mysteries of his divinity to few (that is, to the disciples alone); but after his resurrection he preached outside, because, when the Holy Spirit had been sent from above, he openly declared to the world through the apostles that he was the Son of God.
VERANUS. How did he utter his voice in the streets?

SALONIUS. Because what he had earlier taught in secret and in hiding, and to the one people of the Jews only, he afterwards preaches openly through the apostles across the breadth of the peoples and before all the nations, in accordance with what he commanded them, saying: What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light, that is, openly; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the rooftops, that is, plainly and before all.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: At the head of the crowds she cries out?

SALONIUS. By 'head' the rulers of the Jews are meant. He cried out at the head of the crowds, because through the apostles he openly brought back to the memory of the rulers of the Jews the murder they had committed against him, and called them to the remedy of penance.
VERANUS. How is what follows to be understood: At the doors of the city gates she utters her words?

SALONIUS. By the city is meant the holy Church, gathered from both peoples, namely the Jews and the gentiles. The doors of the gates of this city were the holy teachers, who by preaching the word of the Gospel led believers into it. Wisdom, then, uttered her words at the doors of the city gates when Christ spoke in his apostles.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: Incline your heart to understand prudence (Prov. 2)? How can a man incline his heart?
SALONIUS. He inclines his heart to know prudence who humbles himself and cleanses his mind of sins, so as to become worthy to receive the mysteries of the Godhead.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: Do not lean on your own wisdom? For who leans on wisdom?
SALONIUS. He who trusts that by his own wisdom or his own strength he can fulfil the divine commandments.
VERANUS. See, again he says: Do not be wise in your own eyes (Prov. 3). For who is wise in his own eyes?
SALONIUS. Surely he who exalts himself above others as a teacher, and boasts of what he has been able to know and understand rightly from the sayings of the Fathers.
VERANUS. What is a man's true wisdom?
SALONIUS. To fear the Lord and depart from evil; and this is what follows straight after: Fear the Lord, and depart from evil.
VERANUS. How do you know that this is a man's true wisdom?
SALONIUS. Because in the book of Job it is written: See, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil, understanding.
VERANUS. Who is that man of whom Solomon says: Blessed is the man who finds wisdom?
SALONIUS. The faithful and catholic Christian.
VERANUS. When does he find wisdom?
SALONIUS. When he receives the teaching of truth, that is, of the Gospel, with body and heart together, and is eager to learn the will of the Lord in the holy Scriptures.
VERANUS. When does prudence abound?
SALONIUS. When with great love and affection for his Creator he hears the divine precepts and is eager to fulfil them in deed.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: Her ways are beautiful, all her paths are peaceful? What are these ways of wisdom, or what are her paths?

SALONIUS. The ways of wisdom are the actions of the Lord which he performed in the flesh, or his teachings which are contained in the books of the Gospel; these ways are beautiful because they are divine. The paths of wisdom are the precepts and commandments of the Lord, which [lead] to eternal peace: peaceful, because all the precepts of the Lord lead to eternal peace.
VERANUS. Of what law or of what counsel does Solomon speak when he says: Keep the law and counsel?
SALONIUS. Of the law and counsel, namely, of the wisdom of the Lord Jesus Christ.
VERANUS. What is the law of wisdom?

SALONIUS. The law of wisdom is that which says: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments, that is, you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal (Matt. 19; Mark 10; Luke 18).
VERANUS. What is the counsel of wisdom?
SALONIUS. If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, and give to the poor.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: Every mocker is an abomination to the Lord? Who is a mocker?

SALONIUS. A mocker is one who corrupts the words of God by understanding and teaching them perversely. A mocker is one who scorns his simple and poor neighbours by insulting them. A mocker is one who looks down on the great promises of God as if they were small, and spurns the punishment of eternal damnation as if it were bearable. The Lord abhors all such people, and his converse is with the simple, because the grace of heavenly wisdom enlightens them, since they have nothing double in themselves.

VERANUS. Why does Solomon say: And I too was my father's son, tender and only-begotten in the sight of my mother (Prov. 4)? How was he only-begotten in the sight of his mother, when a brother by the same mother preceded him, as the holy Scripture of the book of Kings (2 Kings 12) testifies?

SALONIUS. It is true that a brother by the same mother preceded him, but that brother soon died: he departed from this life without a name, as if he had never been, and for this reason he calls himself only-begotten.
VERANUS. Why does he say: Do not turn aside to the right or to the left? For who could hold himself so still that he does not turn his body to the right side or to the left?
SALONIUS. No one; but by the right is signified the good way, by the left the bad and reprobate way. He does not forbid walking in the right way, but turning aside to the right.
VERANUS. Who, then, turns aside to the right or to the left?

SALONIUS. The just man turns aside to the right when he presumes on his own justice and his own strength; the unjust man turns aside to the left when, because of the frailty of the flesh, he despairs that he can be saved. He turns aside to the right who wishes to be wiser than he ought to be wise (Rom. 12); he turns aside to the left who serves folly.
VERANUS. Why then does he say a little further on: The Lord knows the ways that are on the right?

SALONIUS. By the ways that are on the right are signified holy actions and good works: for these the Lord knows, that is, he directs them, and they please him. Hence, on the other hand, he will say to the reprobate at the judgement: I do not know you: that is, I have not chosen you, for you do not please me, because I do not see you in my light, I do not see you in my justice.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: Do not give your honour to strangers, and your years to the cruel one (Prov. 5)? Of what honour does he speak, or whom does he call strangers?

SALONIUS. He speaks of the honour that man was made in the image of God; he calls the demons strangers, and the sense is: Do not, by living badly, subject your honour, that you were created in the image of God, to unclean spirits.
VERANUS. Whom does he call the cruel one, or of what years does he speak?
SALONIUS. He calls the spans of life years, and the devil the cruel one, and the sense is: Do not, by living badly, hand over to the devil the spans of life that God has given you.
VERANUS. From what cistern does Solomon teach us to drink water, or from what well the streams, when he says: Drink water from your own cistern, and the streams of your own well?

SALONIUS. He calls the catholic doctrine, that is, [the doctrine] of the Old and New Testament, a cistern; and the depth and height of that same catholic doctrine a well; knowledge, water; by streams he means the plenty and abundance of knowledge, that is, the various senses of holy Scripture. For by these words he teaches us to beware of the doctrine of heretics and to attend to the readings of the holy Scriptures, and the sense is: Drink water from your own cistern, that is, keep and fulfil in deed the doctrine which you preach to others. And the streams of your own well: that is, let the abundance of your speech, or of your knowledge, flow back into you abundantly in good works.

VERANUS. Why does Solomon say: Let your springs be channelled outside, and divide your waters in the streets, when he immediately adds: Keep them to yourself alone, so that strangers may not be your partners? If we channel our springs outside and divide our waters in the streets, how can we keep them to ourselves alone?

SALONIUS. Although it may seem so from the sound of the words, there is nevertheless no contradiction, because these sayings cannot be understood except spiritually. We channel our springs outside, then, when we pour the power of preaching into others, when we proclaim the words of holy Scripture to others. We divide our waters in the streets when we preach to the peoples. For a street [platea] is named from breadth; for it is a Greek word. We divide our waters in the streets, then, when we spread the words of knowledge broadly among a multitude of hearers and dispense the divine utterances according to the character of each one.
VERANUS. If we ought to divide our waters in the streets, how then can we keep them to ourselves alone?
SALONIUS. We divide our waters in the streets when we preach the divine words widely to others, and yet we keep the waters to ourselves alone, because we do not seek human praise from that preaching.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: So that strangers may not be your partners (Prov. 5:17)?

SALONIUS. He calls the demons strangers, of whom the Psalmist said: Strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my life (Ps. 53:5), etc. For we make the malignant, that is, the unclean spirits, partners and companions with us in preaching when we swell up through pride and desire empty glory from our preaching.
VERANUS. Of what man does Solomon say: For the apostate, a useless man, walks with a perverse mouth (Prov. 6)?
SALONIUS. He calls the schismatic, who labours to split the unity of the Church, an apostate man.
VERANUS. In what language is he called an apostate?
SALONIUS. In Greek; which is interpreted in the Latin tongue as a deserter, one who withdraws from the truth.
VERANUS. Why then is a schismatic called an apostate?

SALONIUS. Because, after the manner of the proud angel, he first swells up within and falls from the standing of his own mind, since in this way he withdraws from the love of his Creator and from the truth: for unless he first withdrew from the truth, he would not sow injustice in the Church.
VERANUS. Why then is it said of him: He winks with his eyes, he treads with his foot, he speaks with his finger?

SALONIUS. It is the inner guard of the mind that keeps the members outwardly in order: this apostate, then, because he has lost his standing and guard, therefore has his outward members [...] disordered.
VERANUS. What is it that he says of his law: Bind it on your fingers, write it on the tablets of your heart (Prov. 7)? For who can bind the law on his fingers, or if he did, what use would it be?

SALONIUS. On the fingers, he says, that is, in actions: for whoever strives to fulfil and adorn the law in good works binds it on his fingers. On the tablets of the heart, he says, that is, in the breadth of thought. He writes the law on the tablets of his heart, then, who receives it with joy and commits it to memory.
VERANUS. What is it that Wisdom says: Through me kings reign, and the makers of law decree just things; through me princes rule, and the mighty decree justice?
SALONIUS. [This is] Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.
VERANUS. Does Christ, then, give kingdom and rule to all impious tyrants and princes?

SALONIUS. Certainly not; yet by his permission impious kings and princes take up kingdoms or empires, for it is written in the book of Job: He permits a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people (Job 34). But in this place he calls the holy apostles kings, who knew how to rule faithfully first themselves, and then the Church entrusted to them. Or he calls kings all the saints, who know how to rule themselves and others well.
VERANUS. Whom does he call makers of laws?
SALONIUS. The writers of both Testaments.
VERANUS. Whom does he call princes and the mighty?

SALONIUS. The other teachers and rulers of the faithful: for all these had kingdom, principality and rule through the wisdom of God the Father; that is, they received it through Christ that they might be something good, whence he himself says: Without me you can do nothing (John 15).
VERANUS. What is it that Wisdom says: I was delighted every day, playing before him?
SALONIUS. That is, playing before the Father at all times in the world.
VERANUS. Did Wisdom, that is, the Son of God, play childishly before the Father?

SALONIUS. Far from it: but where he says playing, it is to be understood as rejoicing. For he played every day, that is, he rejoiced that he was one, that is, of one substance with the Father, from the beginning, from the days of eternity.
VERANUS. How did he play at all times in the world?
SALONIUS. Because when the times of the world and creatures began to be, the Son himself rejoiced, because what he himself was always remained in the Father.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: Wisdom has built herself a house (Prov. 9), and what house did she build herself?
SALONIUS. Wisdom, that is, the Son of God, built himself a house, since he himself created a man in the womb of the Virgin, whom he assumed into the unity of his person.
VERANUS. How did she hew out seven pillars?

SALONIUS. She hewed out seven pillars because through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit she raised up churches throughout the world, which, like pillars, by supporting [it] hold the memory of him, that is, the mystery of his Incarnation.
VERANUS. Can it be understood otherwise?

SALONIUS. Indeed it can: the house of Wisdom is the Church of Christ; the pillars of this house are the holy teachers; and these pillars are rightly said to be seven, because the holy teachers are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.
VERANUS. How then did Wisdom hew out these pillars?
SALONIUS. She hewed out the pillars because she separated the minds of preachers from love of the present world, and raised them up to bear the structure of that same Church.
VERANUS. Of what maidservants does he speak a little further on: She sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and to the walls of the city (Prov. 9)?
SALONIUS. He calls the holy apostles maidservants.
VERANUS. Why does he call them maidservants?

SALONIUS. On account of their lack of learning, their weakness and their poverty; for he chose as apostles the unlettered, the weak, the poor and the despised, whom he sent into the world to preach, so that they might call the faithful peoples to the citadel of eternal blessedness and to the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem.
VERANUS. Who is the wise son who gladdens his father; or who is the foolish son who is a grief to his mother?

SALONIUS. He who keeps well the mysteries of faith and baptism he has received and fulfils them in deed is a wise son; he without doubt gladdens God the Father. But he who corrupts the sacraments of faith and baptism he has received with evil works or heretical depravity is a foolish son; he indeed is a grief to his mother, that is, the Church, because he saddens her.
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: The fool will be beaten by his lips? How can a foolish man be beaten by his lips?

SALONIUS. Beating in this place signifies damnation. The fool, then, will be beaten by his lips, because he will be condemned for the wicked and evil words he has spoken. Hence Moses (better, Solomon) also says elsewhere: And life is in the hands of the tongue (Prov. 18), since each one will either be condemned by his words or be justified by his words (Matt. 12).
VERANUS. Why is the tongue said to have hands, when it cannot have hands?

SALONIUS. It is said metaphorically, that is, by transference, just as the winds are said to have wings (Ps. 17, 103, etc.): for the hands of the tongue are the words themselves, by which [a person] either earns life by speaking good things or earns death by speaking evil things. Otherwise, in the sacred Scriptures works are often signified by hands, as in this: For you shall eat the labours of your hands (Ps. 127). He says in the hands of the tongue, that is, in its works. For the works of the tongue are good or evil conversations, from which death or life arises.
VERANUS. Who is that sluggard of whom it is said: As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who sent him (Prov. 10:26)?

SALONIUS. The sluggard is a Catholic of evil life who neither labours nor works so as to earn arrival at eternal blessedness. By vinegar and smoke the perfidy of heretics is signified. By the eyes and teeth, the preachers of holy Church, who are well called eyes, because they foresee the right paths; and fittingly also teeth, since they are accustomed to supply spiritual food to the faithful. So as vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, that is, as the perfidy of heretics is opposed to good teachers, because it saddens them and brings them distress and tears, so the sluggard, that is, the bad Catholic, is burdensome to those same good teachers who sent him, that is, who commanded him to fulfil his faith in works. And he is the more burdensome because he destroys his faith with depraved works.
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: Hand in hand, the evil man will not be innocent (Prov. 11:21)? How is an evil man hand in hand, and therefore not innocent?

SALONIUS. He who joins hand to hand certainly does no work. So the evil man, as long as he is hand in hand, will not be innocent, because even if for a time he withdraws his hands from evil work, yet as long as he is evil he cannot have innocence of heart; hence he says above: A perverse heart is abominable to the Lord (Prov. 11:20).
VERANUS. What then is hand in hand?
SALONIUS. A depraved conscience in evil work.
VERANUS. How is what he says to be understood: A golden ring in its nostrils, a woman beautiful and foolish?

SALONIUS. Just as, if you fix a golden ring in its nostrils, that is, in the nostrils of a pig, it, while it goes on turning over and digging the earth with its snout, plunges the golden ring into the wallow of mud, and then the golden ring loses the beauty it had: so likewise a foolish woman, if she has beauty of face, or if she receives ornaments of earrings, necklaces and garments too, soils her beauty and loses her comeliness, if she loves to defile herself in the filth of lust and corrupts herself with adulteries.
VERANUS. But how is this saying to be understood spiritually?

SALONIUS. Whoever meditates attentively on the sacred Scriptures and continually searches the divine utterances receives the ornaments of knowledge. But if by living badly he corrupts and destroys what he understands well, he has a golden ring in his nostrils; but like a pig he digs the earth, defiles [the ring] and plunges it in mud, because he has soiled with unclean conduct the ornament he had gained through knowledge of the Scriptures. Such a soul is a woman beautiful and foolish: beautiful through knowledge, but, given over to carnal delights, she is foolish through her conduct.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: The soul that blesses will be made fat, and he who makes drunk will himself also be made drunk? For there are many who make others drunk, but are not themselves made drunk.

SALONIUS. He does not say this of bodily drunkenness, but of the spiritual soul, which, if it blesses, will be made fat, because whatever [soul] blesses outwardly by preaching receives spiritual blessing, that is, it is increased and grows in spiritual grace. Likewise he who strives to inebriate the minds of his hearers with sacred speech is himself inebriated too, and is filled with the infusion of the Holy Spirit.
VERANUS. Why did he not say: The man, but: The soul that blesses will be made fat?

SALONIUS. In the divine Scriptures the part is quite often put for the whole, or the whole for the part, according to a figure of the art of grammar which is called synecdoche: so in this place the part is put for the whole man. The whole is put for the part, as in this: They have taken the Lord from the tomb (John 20). He says the Lord, for the body of the Lord.
VERANUS. Who is he of whom he says: He who hides grain will be cursed among the peoples (Prov. 11)? Is anyone to be cursed because he does not supply his grain to everyone?

SALONIUS. The grain is the words of holy preaching: so whoever hides this grain, that is, keeps the words of holy preaching to himself and will not announce [these] utterances to others, he will be cursed among the peoples, because he will be condemned for the fault of silence, since he could have benefited many; but because he would not, he will therefore justly be punished for the penalty of many.
VERANUS. Who are those who sell grain, of whom it follows soon after: But blessing upon the heads of those who sell?
SALONIUS. Those sell grain who announce the words of life and of holy preaching to their hearers.
VERANUS. What price do they receive from them?
SALONIUS. The price of faith and holy confession.
VERANUS. How will blessing come upon their heads?
SALONIUS. Because the Lord will say to each of them: Well done, good and faithful servant, because (Matt. 25), etc.
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: He who troubles his house will possess the winds? How can anyone possess the winds?

SALONIUS. In this place he calls the mind a house, in which each one dwells through his thoughts as in a house; he calls unclean spirits winds. So he who does not fear to disturb his house, that is, his mind, with evil and harmful thoughts, he indeed will possess the winds, because through evil thoughts he has made a way for demons to enter and dwell in him. He will possess the winds, that is, demons, to his own condemnation.
VERANUS. How is a diligent woman a crown to her husband, and she who does things worthy of shame rottenness in his bones (Prov. 12)?

SALONIUS. A good and chaste woman offers honour to her husband in all things; and because she loves him and manages his house well, she is a crown to him, because she adds grace to his virtues, whence he is crowned by the Lord. But an adulterous woman, though outwardly she seems handsome, is yet rottenness in the bones, because inwardly she defiles [his] members with the stench of her lust.
VERANUS. How is what he says to be understood: Better is the poor man who is sufficient for himself than the glorious man who lacks bread?

SALONIUS. Truly better is an unlettered and simple brother who does the good things he knows, whereby he earns eternal life in heaven, than the glorious man, that is, one famous for teaching and learning in the Scriptures, or adorned with the office of teacher, who lacks the bread of love, because he loves neither the Lord nor his neighbour. Or surely he lacks bread for this reason, that he does not practise what he understands or teaches.
VERANUS. Who is the shrewd man who conceals knowledge? For so he says: The shrewd man conceals knowledge.

SALONIUS. Shrewd is used in this place in a good sense, that is, wise and prudent. So the shrewd man, that is, the wise and prudent man, sometimes deliberately conceals knowledge, namely for two reasons: one, because he cannot speak to weak hearers as to spiritual people, but as to carnal ones (1 Cor. 3), that is, he does not dare to reveal to them the great mysteries of the sacred Scriptures which he knows, lest perhaps they be scandalised; the other, because he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs, nor to cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7).
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: The sluggard wills and does not will (Prov. 13)? If he wills, how then does he not will?

SALONIUS. By the sluggard is meant the one who does not wish to exert himself in good works. So the sluggard wishes to reign with God, and does not wish to labour for God. He wishes to reach blessedness, and yet he does not wish to fulfil the commandments of Christ, so that he may earn the attainment of blessedness. For of this man James says: A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways (James 1).
VERANUS. Of which workers does he say: But the soul of those who work shall be made fat (Prov. 13)?
SALONIUS. He speaks of those who do good works, who strive to fulfil the Lord's commandments; their soul will be made fat with spiritual grace and with the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom.
VERANUS. Why will the soul of those who do good works be made fat?
SALONIUS. Because after the labours of the present life it will be rewarded with an unfading recompense.
VERANUS. Who is the messenger of the wicked one, of whom he says: The messenger of the wicked one falls into evil?

SALONIUS. The messenger of the wicked one, that is, the angel of the devil. Arius and Sabellius and the other heretics were angels of Satan; these indeed fell into evil, that is, the torment of eternal Gehenna.
VERANUS. Who is the faithful envoy, of whom there follows: A faithful envoy is health (Prov. 13)?
SALONIUS. The faithful envoy is every catholic preacher and teacher who gains health and eternal salvation for himself and for his hearers.

VERANUS. Why does he say: The evil will lie before the good, and the wicked before the gates of the just, when in this life it is rather the good who usually lie before the evil, and the just before the gates of the wicked?

SALONIUS. At the last judgement, when the just have been crowned, the wicked who afflicted them in the present life will be condemned, and that is why he says: The evil will lie before the good, and the wicked before the gates of the just. Yet his saying 'before the good' and 'before the gates of the just' does not concern nearness of place, since the evil and the good will not then be near each other; but it concerns the sight of the good, since the good will always see the torments of the evil, so that they may give greater thanks without end to God their deliverer.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: Weight and balance are the judgements of the Lord, and all the stones of the world are his works (Prov. 16)? How are weight and balance the judgements of the Lord?

SALONIUS. Because the Lord has ordered all things in weight and measure and number (Wisd. 11). Weight and balance are the Lord's judgements, because, just as he willed, he has distributed to each one the measure of faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit.
VERANUS. Whom does he call the stones of the world?

SALONIUS. The just and those strong in faith. For all the stones of the world, that is, the holy and elect men, are the works of the Lord, because no one by his own strength, no one by his own merit, has been chosen by the Lord to be fit for the heavenly building, but by his grace and mercy alone.
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: The crown of old men is their sons' sons, and the glory of sons is their fathers (Prov. 17)? If the sons' sons are wicked, how are they a glory in this place?

SALONIUS. He means the patriarchs and prophets, whose sons are the holy apostles, and the sons' sons the successors of the apostles, namely the holy preachers. For all these are the crown of the old men, that is, of the patriarchs and prophets, because they celebrate with fitting praise those through whose examples and prophecies they came to the knowledge of grace.
VERANUS. How are the fathers [the glory] of the sons?
SALONIUS. It is indeed a great glory for the preachers of the New Testament that they have been found worthy to be sons of the ancient fathers, that is, of the patriarchs and prophets.

VERANUS. Why does he say: He who lets out water is the source of quarrels? Does the man who lets dammed water run off stir up quarrels? Or is it not wine rather than water that usually stirs up quarrels?

SALONIUS. This is said figuratively: for by water is meant a light and loose tongue; and he who gives his tongue free rein beyond measure is the source of quarrels, because he who does not bridle his tongue stirs up quarrels and disputes and destroys concord.
VERANUS. Tell me, I ask, how wisdom shines in the face of the prudent man, as Solomon says: But the eyes of fools are on the ends of the earth?

SALONIUS. A prudent man often shows beforehand, in the very brightness of his countenance, the gravity of his mind and the clarity of his understanding. But fools cannot raise the eyes of the mind to imitate and pursue this, namely gravity, but search with all their wonder how they may reach the end (that is, the fulfilment of carnal pleasures).
VERANUS. Ought we to understand it only in this way?

SALONIUS. We ought to understand this as said especially of Christ. For in the face of the prudent man (namely the Saviour) shone the wisdom of the Godhead, which he, appearing in the flesh, displayed and confirmed by the testimony of his mighty works and teaching. But the eyes of fools (that is, of the unbelieving Jews) were inflamed more by earthly desires than by his saving admonitions and teachings.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: A man's gift enlarges his way, and makes room for him before princes (Prov. 18)? What is this gift that enlarges a man's way, and makes room for him before princes?

SALONIUS. This gift is the gift of love, or of the other virtues which the faithful receive from the Lord: this gift of a man, namely, enlarges his way, that is, his action; because the more fully each believer is filled within by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the more he enlarges his way outwardly, that is, multiplies the steps of good works, because daily he grows and increases in holy desires and good works.
VERANUS. How does this gift make room for a man before princes?
SALONIUS. Because among the great rulers of the Church it grants him, in the forum, the height of honour and the glory of eternal blessedness.

VERANUS. Why does he say: The sluggard hides his hand under his armpit, and does not bring it to his mouth (Prov. 19 and 26)? For who is so sluggish that, when eating or drinking, he does not bring his hand to his mouth?

SALONIUS. He who hides his hand under his armpit certainly does not wish to stretch it out to any work or labour. So by the sluggard is meant every slack and idle preacher who does not wish to fulfil in deed what he says; for he stretches his hand to his mouth who strives to fulfil in deed what he teaches.

VERANUS. Who is that sluggard of whom he says: Because of the cold the sluggard would not plough; therefore he will beg in summer, and it will not be given him (Prov. 20)? But if the sluggard would not plough in the time of cold, will he not be able, in the time of summer, to find someone to give him something?

SALONIUS. Indeed sluggards often find, both in time of cold and of summer, faithful people to give them alms. But the sluggard in this place signifies the one who, through idleness and the adversity of this world (which is meant by the cold), neglects to labour in the service of God, and therefore on the future day of judgement he will beg, because he will not have good works for which he may deserve to receive blessedness, since whatever a man sows, that he will also reap (Gal. 6).
VERANUS. Why then are the day of judgement and the kingdom of God compared to summer?
SALONIUS. Because then all the clouds of our sorrow will pass away, and the day of that life will shine with the brightness of the eternal sun.
VERANUS. Of what king does he say: The king who sits on the throne of judgement scatters all evil with his gaze?

SALONIUS. Of him who is King of kings and Lord of lords, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who sits on the throne of judgement, because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son (John 5). He indeed scatters all evil with his gaze, because by the regard of his power he will penetrate all evil, even of secret thoughts, so as to render to each according to what he has done; whence he says in the Gospel: Nothing is so covered that it will not be revealed, or hidden that it will not be known (Luke 12). Then, when the just have been crowned with the Lord, the reprobate alone will undergo eternal punishments.
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: Weight and weight, measure and measure, both are abominable to God (Prov. 20 and 21)?

SALONIUS. By weight and weight, measure and measure, he means a differing weight and a differing measure. So as far as the letter goes, whoever has in his house a varying weight and a varying measure surely has it for this purpose, that he may weigh and measure one way for himself and another way for his neighbour, which is surely abominable to the Lord; whence in the law of Moses the Lord commanded, saying: Let your bushel be fair, and your pint just (Lev. 19).
VERANUS. But how should it be understood spiritually?

SALONIUS. He has in his house a differing weight and a differing measure who always seeks in his own actions something for which he may be praised, and searches in the actions of others for something for which they may be blamed. Such a man is surely abominable to God, for the more he desires to please himself, the more he displeases God, who searches out all the secrets of the heart.
VERANUS. How is what he says to be understood: It is bad, it is bad, says every buyer, and when he has gone away, then he will boast (Prov. 20)?
SALONIUS. According to the letter, a buyer usually finds fault with what he wants to buy, and says: It is bad, it is bad; yet if he has bought well, he will boast when he has gone away.
VERANUS. But how do you understand it spiritually?

SALONIUS. He is truly a buyer who desires to obtain for himself eternal rewards in heaven. He indeed strives to buy heavenly things with earthly, lasting things with perishable, eternal things with temporal. Such a buyer, then, says that whatever he suffers in the present is bad, because he understands it to be bad. Yet because he patiently endures all adversities for God's sake, when he has withdrawn from the world, then he will boast, because he will come to blessedness.
VERANUS. Likewise, how is what he says a little later to be understood: An inheritance that is hastened after in the beginning will lack blessing at the last?

SALONIUS. This inheritance can be understood as the acquisition of avarice: so whoever desire to multiply riches for themselves in this life through the wickedness of avarice must in the future lose the blessedness of the eternal inheritance. Otherwise: whoever desire to seek human praise for good works hasten in the beginning as if to an inheritance; and so at the last they will lack blessing, because they will receive no reward from God; for of such it is written: Amen I say to you, they have received their reward (Matt. 6:2, 5).
VERANUS. What is it that he says: It is a man's ruin to devour the saints, and after vows to deal [with them] (Prov. 20)? What is this, to devour the saints?

SALONIUS. To devour the saints is to bind oneself by a vow. The wicked devoured the saints when they bound themselves by a vow to persecute the saints and kill them, as forty Jewish men did, as is told in the Acts of the Apostles: They vowed that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul (Acts 23). And the pagans, as we often read, vowed the blood of Christians to their gods.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: And after vows to deal [with them] (Prov. 20)?
SALONIUS. To deal again after promised vows is to persecute the saint and tear him apart, and to despise him like a worthless slave.
VERANUS. How then is it a man's ruin to devour the saints, and after vows to deal [with them]?

SALONIUS. For if it is a sin to harm any man, it is much more a sin when someone persecutes or offends or injures the saints of God; and therefore it is ruin to him who, by persecuting the saints, prepares for himself the destruction of eternal damnation.

VERANUS. How is what he says to be understood: Like the divisions of waters, so is the king's heart in the hand of God? Why did he say that only the king's heart is in the hand of God, and not [the hearts] of all men, when it is written elsewhere: In his hand are all the ends of the earth (Ps. 94); if all the ends of the earth are in God's power, are not the hearts of all men also in his hand?

SALONIUS. In this place we should not understand as king him who is king in name only and rules others in temporal things, but every holy man, a faithful and devout Christian, whose soldiers are the sacred virtues, and who knows how to win well the wars of the vices within himself. Just as God, then, by manifold divisions of waters fills far and wide the ends of the lands and of the air, so he will incline the king's heart wherever he wills, that is, he will turn it to whatever good he wills: for just as he grants divisions of graces to angels and men according to his will, so he fills the hearts of kings (that is, of the saints) with various gifts, and adorns them with diverse endowments.

VERANUS. What is it that he says: A man who has strayed from the way of teaching will dwell in the assembly of the giants (Prov. 21)? Who are these giants, in whose assembly he who has strayed from the way of teaching will dwell?

SALONIUS. He called the unclean spirits giants, that is, demons, of whom blessed Job says: Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters, and those who dwell with them (Job 26), that is, the demons and all whom they have deceived, and who consented to them, are tormented in punishments.
VERANUS. Why are demons called giants?

SALONIUS. Because demons are proud and haughty, and wicked and strong, as the giants once were. In the assembly of these giants, then, that is, of the demons, all will dwell who have strayed from the way of teaching, that is, from the way of truth; because they will be tormented together with the demons in the punishment of eternal damnation.
VERANUS. What is the city of the strong, or who is the wise man of whom he says: The wise man went up into the city of the strong, and pulled down the strength of its confidence (Prov. 21)?

SALONIUS. He calls the world the city; the demons, the strong. This world was once the city of the strong, because, given over to the worship of idols, it served demons, and had confidence of life in the worship of those who are not gods, but the works of men's hands.
VERANUS. Who then is that wise man who went up into this city of the strong?

SALONIUS. The Son of the Virgin, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who went up into this city when, born in the flesh, he appeared visible to the world. He indeed destroyed the strength of its confidence, because he overthrew and removed from the world the worship of the gods in whom the gentiles trusted.

VERANUS. What is it that the proverb says: A youth according to his way, even when he has grown old, will not depart from it (Prov. 22)? Do not many depart from the evil way which they walked in youth?

SALONIUS. Truly very many, by the inspiration of divine grace, are converted in old age from the vices they had in youth; nor does Solomon deny that this can happen: but it more often tends to happen that a man does not change in old age the habits he learns in youth; yet he does not affirm that it always turns out so, and therefore he sets down a proverb of this kind to admonish everyone to strive to labour at virtues and good works from their earliest age, lest perhaps in old age they be unable to learn the pursuits of good works which they neglected at a tender age.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: The mouth of the strange woman is a deep pit (Prov. 22 and 23)? Who is this strange woman, whose mouth is a great pit?

SALONIUS. By the mouth of the strange woman he means the mouth of a harlot: so whoever gladly listens to a harlot's words and receives her kisses with delight knocks, as it were, at the door of the deep pit, that is, of hell, and unless he quickly withdraws himself from her talk or kiss, God abandoning him, he is at once plunged into the pit of death: and this is what he says: He with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it.

VERANUS. What is it that he says: Apply your heart to my teaching? And a little later he adds: Behold, I have described it to you in three ways, in thoughts and knowledge, that I might show you the certainty and the words of truth (Prov. 22). How did he describe his teaching and knowledge in three ways? Or what is it to apply and understand teaching?
SALONIUS. He indeed describes his teaching in three ways who commands each person to strive to fulfil it in thought, word and deed.
VERANUS. Of what boundaries does he speak: Do not pass over the ancient boundaries which your fathers set (Prov. 23:28)?

SALONIUS. By ancient boundaries he means the boundaries of truth and faith which the catholic teachers established from the beginning. He commanded this, then, that no one should receive the truth of the sacred faith and of the gospel teaching otherwise than it was handed down by the holy Fathers. Or he commanded this, that no one should interpret the words of the holy Scriptures otherwise than according to the intention of each writer.

VERANUS. What are those riches of which he says: Do not lift up your eyes to riches which you cannot have, for they will make themselves wings and fly into heaven? What wings can riches, that is, wealth or abundance, make for themselves?

SALONIUS. These riches are the hidden things of the Godhead and the secrets of the heavenly mysteries, and the sense is: Do not lift up the eyes of your mind to search out the hidden things of the Godhead and the secrets of the heavenly mysteries, which you cannot penetrate nor are able to understand, since these lie open to eagles alone, that is, they are manifest only to the citizens on high.
VERANUS. What are the storerooms of which he says: By teaching the storerooms will be filled, all substance, both precious and most beautiful (Prov. 24)?

SALONIUS. The storerooms are the hearts of the righteous, which through the teaching of wisdom are filled with precious and most beautiful substance, that is, with the gifts of virtues and of good works.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: For the righteous man will fall seven times, and will rise again; if he is righteous, how is he said to fall, that is, to sin?

SALONIUS. Solomon speaks here of light and daily sins, without which none of the righteous could be, or can be, in this life; as it says elsewhere: I will bless the Lord at all times seven times (Ps. 33): [seven times] also sometimes means often and frequently, which can very fittingly be understood here: seven times, that is, often, the righteous man will fall, and often will rise again: or certainly at all times he falls and rises, namely by divine grace, according to what was said above.
VERANUS. How is this to be understood: Prepare your work outside, and diligently till your field, so that afterwards you may build your house? What is it that we ought to prepare outside?

SALONIUS. He calls a good action a work, and therefore he added, your; that is, useful and necessary to you. So we prepare our work outside when we arrange our action well outwardly and order it so that it may please God.
VERANUS. How do we diligently till our field?
SALONIUS. We diligently till the field if we clear our body of the thorns of vices.
VERANUS. After tilling the field, how shall we build our house?

SALONIUS. If we first arrange our outward acts well, we build a house well for ourselves when we keep purity of life and cleanness even of thoughts, and adorn the dwelling of our mind with devout thoughts.
VERANUS. Who is the Lord, or who are the kings, of whom he says: It is the glory of the Lord to conceal the word; the glory of kings to search out the saying (Prov. 25:2)?

SALONIUS. This Lord is the Son of God, namely the Lord Jesus, whose glory it was to conceal the word, that is, that he was the Son of God: for while he appeared in the flesh, he wished to profess himself a man rather than the Son of God, so that the devil should not recognise him, and so by his passion he might redeem the human race: since if the devil had recognised that he was the Son of God, he would never have crucified [him]. So it was the glory of the Lord to conceal the word, that is, in the form of a man to hide the power of his divinity, so that, while he showed the weakness of the flesh, the devil should not hasten to draw him back from the passion, so that through [the devil's] ignorance [he might proceed] through the passion to the glory of the resurrection.
VERANUS. Who then are the kings whose glory is to search out the saying?

SALONIUS. These kings were the holy apostles, who diligently strove to search out the saying of the Lord by which he signified that he was the Lord. For where he did not show openly that he was the Lord, but wished to be understood mystically, they examined his saying with the greatest diligence, such as this, etc.: I and the Father are one (John 10). For when he was concealing the divinity of the Word and showing the weakness of the flesh, he questioned these kings, saying: Whom do men say the Son of Man is? To him the foremost of the kings, namely blessed Peter the apostle, searching out his saying, which he had often heard before, at once replied: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.
VERANUS. What is it that follows: Heaven above, and earth below, and the heart of kings, they say, is unsearchable (Prov. 25)?

SALONIUS. He calls the prophets and apostles kings, who, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, were found worthy to know the secrets of the Godhead. By the heart of kings is signified the knowledge and understanding of the prophets and apostles.
VERANUS. How then is what he says to be understood: Heaven above, and earth below, and the heart of kings unsearchable?

SALONIUS. Just as the height of heaven and the depth of the earth cannot be grasped by men, so our capacity is not able to grasp, or to penetrate, the height of the knowledge and understanding of the prophets and apostles.

VERANUS. How do they agree with each other, or how can they be consistent with each other, the things he says: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him, and, Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem to himself to be wise (Prov. 26)? These sentences certainly seem to be strongly contrary to each other.

SALONIUS. Truly they agree well with each other, if we consider them carefully. For by saying, Do not answer a fool according to his folly, he admonishes us that, since the fool does not grasp wisdom, we should not imitate his folly, but rather scorn and despise it; and whenever we speak to him, we should speak not shamefully, not furiously, not proudly, but decently, patiently and humbly, and wisely, lest we become like him. But by what follows, Answer a fool according to his folly, he admonishes us to rebuke and refute the fool wisely, and to show plainly how great the folly in him is, lest perhaps, if he does not recognise his folly, he think himself wise.
VERANUS. Who is that whisperer of whom he says: The words of the whisperer [seem] simple, and they reach the inner parts of the belly?

SALONIUS. He calls the whisperer the instigator of strife and the double-tongued man, who feigns praise in his words, and therefore his words seem as if simple. But they reach the inner parts of the belly, because the whisperer always seeks to hear something from which he can sow quarrels, at which the stomach is angered and all the inner parts are thrown into turmoil.
VERANUS. What is that hidden love of which he says: Better is open rebuke than hidden love (Prov. 27)?

SALONIUS. Hidden love in this place he calls unlawful love, that is, lustful, such as adulterous love, which is hidden because of its shamefulness, lest it be refuted by the wise. So open rebuke is better than hidden love, because it is much better to rebuke someone openly so that he may be corrected than to love him secretly with the aim of sinning together.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: A sated soul will trample the honeycomb; a hungry soul will take the bitter for sweet? How does a sated soul trample the honeycomb?

SALONIUS. According to the letter, a sated soul tramples the honeycomb, because whoever is filled with food scorns and despises sweet fare; but whoever is hungry thinks little of it even if he takes some bitterness in his food.
VERANUS. But spiritually, how is this sentence to be understood?

SALONIUS. The sated soul is the soul of the rich, who have their consolation in the present life, since they abound in supplies of temporal things. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: Woe to you who are sated, for you will hunger (Luke 6). So the soul of the rich tramples the honeycomb, because for earthly goods it spurns the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom. But the hungry soul will take even the bitter for sweet, since whoever hungers and thirsts for righteousness (Matt. 5) takes all bitterness for sweetness, because he patiently endures every adversity of the present life for love of the sweetness above, that is, of eternal blessedness.
VERANUS. To whom does Solomon speak when he says: Know diligently the face of your cattle, and consider your flocks (Prov. 27)? Surely he is not teaching [us] to consider woolly flocks?

SALONIUS. No: for he speaks to the shepherd of the Church, and the sense is: Bestow care diligently on those over whom you are set, and know the minds and acts of each one; and if you find any filth of vices, strive to chastise and cleanse [it] quickly.
VERANUS. Why does he then add: For you will not have power perpetually, but a crown will be given to generation of generations?

SALONIUS. So that the shepherd of the Church may apply care unceasingly to the sheep entrusted to him; and the sense is: For you will not always have the power of feeding the Lord's sheep, but a crown will be given in the generation of generations, that is, an eternal crown has been prepared, which you too will receive if you have fed the Lord's sheep well.

VERANUS. What need was there for Solomon to say: The meadows are opened, and the green grasses have appeared, and the hay has been gathered from the mountains? For who says this, or is ignorant of it?
SALONIUS. Truly no one, if we take these words only according to the letter.
VERANUS. How then are they to be understood?
SALONIUS. Truly, only spiritually.
VERANUS. What then do the meadows signify?

SALONIUS. By the meadows are signified the heavenly mysteries, which are called meadows because they are the pastures of faithful souls. For these meadows, that is, the divine mysteries, were long closed under the types and figures of the law.
VERANUS. How and when were these meadows opened?

SALONIUS. The meadows were indeed opened, because through the grace of the Lord the Saviour the heavenly sacraments were revealed, when he opened the understanding of his disciples, that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). Then the green grasses also appeared, that is, the new sentences of the truth and glory of the Gospel.
VERANUS. What does the hay that was gathered from the mountains signify?

SALONIUS. By the mountains are signified the holy Fathers, the writers of the Old Testament; by the hay, their writings. The hay was gathered from the mountains, because the writings of the holy ancient Fathers were gathered for the fodder and refreshment of the Lord's sheep, that is, of faithful souls.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: The poor man and the creditor have met each other; the Lord is the enlightener of both (Prov. 29)? Who are this poor man and this creditor who have met each other?
SALONIUS. The poor man is the humble hearer of the word; the creditor is he who, by preaching, entrusts the money of the word of God to the poor man, that is, to the humble hearer.
VERANUS. When do the poor man and the creditor meet each other?

SALONIUS. When hearer and preacher together come into one and the same grace of divine kindness: hence it fittingly follows: The Lord is the enlightener of both (Prov. 29); because without the grace of divine kindness neither could the one preach nor the other believe.
VERANUS. What is it that he says: When prophecy fails, the people will be scattered? What is this prophecy, at whose failing the people will be scattered?

SALONIUS. Prophecy is the learning and teaching of priests: so when the teaching and learning of priests ceases, the people will be scattered; because when the admonition and rebuke of priests is lacking, [the people] is left to its own will and judgement, and is at once corrupted by various sins and vices.
VERANUS. How is every word of God a fiery shield? For Solomon says this: Every word of God is a fiery shield to those who hope in him (Prov. 30)?

SALONIUS. Every word of divine authority is called a fiery shield for this reason: because it both kindles with the fire of brightness the hearts of the elect who place their hope in God, and enlightens them with the knowledge of truth, and consumes and purges the filth of vices which it finds in them, and defends them from the snares of enemies and from all adversities.
VERANUS. What is the leech, which he says has two daughters? For he says this: The leech has two daughters, saying: Bring, and they are never satisfied.
SALONIUS. The leech is the devil, who always thirsts for blood, that is, desires to draw men into sins, and ceaselessly kindles the thirst for sinning.
VERANUS. Who are those two daughters of the leech, saying: Bring, bring, and they are never satisfied?

SALONIUS. Namely lust and avarice: these indeed spiritually imitate the devil's thirst and burning, because just as he is never satisfied with sinning, so neither is avarice nor lust. For the more anyone indulges in lust and fornicates, the more he takes delight [in it]. Likewise, the more anyone heaps up riches for himself, the more he always desires to increase them.
VERANUS. Why did Solomon set forth the example of the gecko, saying: The gecko is fed by hands, and dwells in the houses of the king (ibid.)?
SALONIUS. To rouse the sluggish and those slow of mind to work and to speak well.
VERANUS. What kind of animal is the gecko?
SALONIUS. A kind of lizard, very sluggish and of varied colour; whence it received the name stellio, because it is marked and varied as if with stars (that is, spots).
VERANUS. What then does the gecko signify?

SALONIUS. It signifies those who are slow of mind; and yet by daily study and diligence they climb with their hands to the eternal hall; that is, although with great labour, they come to knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, and are able to penetrate the secrets of the heavenly mysteries. Of such it is written in the Gospel: To him who has it will be given, and he will abound (Matt. 13): since whoever has the zeal for reading, to him will be given the capacity for understanding.
VERANUS. What are those three of which Solomon says: There are three things that walk well, and a fourth that goes along happily?
SALONIUS. The lion, strongest of beasts, who fears the encounter of none; the cock girded about the loins; and the ram, and there is no king who may resist him. These are the things that walk well.
VERANUS. Whom does this lion signify?

SALONIUS. Him of whom it is written: The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, etc. (Rev. 5), namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who is called the strongest of beasts, because what is weak of God is stronger than men (1 Cor. 1).
VERANUS. What is that weakness of God?
SALONIUS. It was a weakness of God to assume the flesh of our mortality: but this is stronger than men, because he himself, a man born of the Virgin, was perfect God.
VERANUS. Why does this lion fear the encounter of none?
SALONIUS. Because he did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2); whence he himself says in the Gospel: Behold, the prince of the world comes, and finds nothing in me.
VERANUS. What does the cock girded about the loins signify?
SALONIUS. The holy preachers.
VERANUS. Why are preachers called cocks?
SALONIUS. Because amid the darkness of the present life they announce by preaching the true morning, that is, the true light, namely the glory of eternal blessedness.
VERANUS. Why are these cocks said to be girded about the loins?
SALONIUS. Because the holy preachers restrain lust and desire in their members.
VERANUS. What does the ram signify, which no king can resist?

SALONIUS. By the ram are designated the holy confessors and priests, who go before the flock like rams, because they lead the faithful people walking by their example. To these rams indeed (if they live spiritually and rightly) there is no king who can resist; because there is no persecutor so savage that he can hinder their purpose, since even if evils are inflicted on them, they bear all things patiently for Christ.
VERANUS. What is that fourth which goes along happily?
SALONIUS. He who appeared foolish after he was raised on high.
VERANUS. Who is he?
SALONIUS. Antichrist, who will be revealed on high, that is, in exaltation: who, though he will be a most wicked man, will deign to name himself the Son of God, and will lie that he is God.
VERANUS. Raised on high, how will he appear foolish?
SALONIUS. Because in his very exaltation and pride he will suddenly be struck by the divine sword and perish.

VERANUS. Why does he say of those earlier ones: There are three things that walk well (Prov. 30), but of this one: A fourth that goes along happily? Why did he not likewise say of this one: He goes along well, but says: happily?
SALONIUS. Because not everything that goes along happily always goes along well, nor does everything that goes along well always [go along] happily.
VERANUS. Which, then, are those that go along well, or which happily?

SALONIUS. Those go along well which walk holily and justly; those go along happily which have their prosperity in this life. The lion, the cock and the ram walk well, but not happily, because Christ too fulfilled the will of God the Father in all things, yet endured many adversities and death: likewise the holy preachers and confessors strive to fulfil the divine will, but endure many persecutions in this life. Antichrist, however, will not go along well, because in his pride he will do everything against God's will: but he will go along happily, because (though for a short time) he will be in great glory and prosperity.
VERANUS. Who is that king Lemuel, of whom he says: The words of King Lemuel, the vision with which his mother instructed him?

SALONIUS. Lemuel is said in the Hebrew language; in Latin it is interpreted 'In whom is God'. He indeed is Solomon, king of Israel, in whom God was; because unless God had dwelt in him, he could neither have understood nor written so many and such great divine mysteries.
VERANUS. Who was his mother, who instructed him and taught [him] the vision?

SALONIUS. According to the letter, his fleshly mother, Queen Bathsheba, can be understood, who taught him wisely; but in this place 'mother' is understood by nothing better than spiritual and divine grace, which instructed him invisibly in his heart and taught [him] the understanding of wisdom, which he himself both preached and wrote outwardly for men.
VERANUS. Who is that strong woman of whom he says: Who will find a strong woman? Far off and from the uttermost borders is her price?

SALONIUS. The holy Catholic Church is called the strong woman; she is called a woman because she bears spiritual sons to God from water and the Holy Spirit. She is called strong because she scorns and despises all the adversities and likewise the prosperities of this world, for the sake of faith in and love of her Maker and Redeemer.
VERANUS. Why did Solomon say: Who will find a strong woman?

SALONIUS. Because he knew through the Holy Spirit that none of the prophets, none at all of the elect, would suffice for the redemption of the human race, except only the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus; and therefore he says: Who will find a strong woman?, understood: except Christ.
VERANUS. Why did he at once add: Far off and from the uttermost borders is her price?

SALONIUS. To show that not in his own time, but long after him, and not like him, Christ was to come, that is, a man pure from the filth of sins; but at the end of the ages the Son was to descend from heaven, who, born of the Virgin, would be perfect God and man: and this is what he says by 'far off', that is, long after. It signifies the time which ran from the days of Solomon to the Virgin's giving birth. He says 'from the uttermost borders' because his going forth is from the highest heaven.
VERANUS. What price did the Lord give for this woman?
SALONIUS. Himself, as the Apostle says: Who loved us, and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice for an odour of sweetness (Eph. 5).
VERANUS. How has the strong woman become like a merchant's ship? For Solomon says this: She has become like a merchant's ship, bringing her bread from afar.

SALONIUS. A merchant (institor) is the name for a trader, because he always presses on (instat) to acquire and multiply his wares and gains. So a merchant's ship, laden with various merchandise which is more abundant in its own country, goes over the sea to foreign places, so that, having sold there all that it brought, it may carry back home dearer goods. So, then, the strong woman, that is, the holy Church, always desires to be laden with the riches of virtues and to abound in good works as she sails over the sea of this world, so that through them she may earn, that is, acquire, greater things, that is, the gifts of divine grace.
VERANUS. Who is the outfitter of this ship?

SALONIUS. The Lord Jesus Christ, who gave the price of his blood and redeemed the Church. So the holy Church, following the example of her outfitter, that is, of her Lord and Redeemer, always labours to multiply for herself the gains of virtues and good works, so that through them she may earn the acquiring of greater things, that is, the rewards of eternal blessedness. And this is what he says: Bringing her bread from afar; because in all the good things she does in time she desires only the strength and fullness of bread, since she awaits only the eternal recompense.
VERANUS. What does it mean to say: She made fine linen and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite (Prov. 31)?

SALONIUS. The Church made fine linen and sold it, because the faith which she had woven by believing she gave by speaking; and from unbelievers she received the faith of right conduct. Therefore she also delivered a girdle to the Canaanite, because by the vigour of the justice she displayed she bound up the loose works of the gentiles, so that what is received may be held fast by living.
VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: She made herself a coverlet garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing? What is a coverlet garment?
SALONIUS. A coverlet garment is one that is usually made very strong with a varied weave.
VERANUS. What, then, is signified by the coverlet garment?

SALONIUS. The strong works of the holy Church and the various ornaments of the virtues, of which the prophet says: The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety (Ps. 44).
VERANUS. How are fine linen and purple the clothing of this woman, that is, of the holy Church?

SALONIUS. Fine linen is a kind of very white flax; hence by fine linen are aptly designated chastity of body and purity of holy conduct, while by purple the shedding of blood is designated. So the strong woman, that is, the holy Church, clothes herself in the fine linen of God, that is, she keeps chastity of body and glows with the brightness of holy conduct. She also clothes herself in purple when in her the holy martyrs shed their blood for the name of Christ.
VERANUS. If fine linen and purple are the clothing of the holy Church, why then does he say in what follows: Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day (Prov. 31)?

SALONIUS. There is no contradiction, because strength refers to the purple, and beauty to the whiteness of the fine linen. So strength is the clothing of the holy Church, because for the faith of Christ and for justice she patiently endures the wickedness and persecution of evil men. And beauty is her clothing, because she works justice and adorns herself with the grace of the virtues.
VERANUS. But why does he say: She will laugh on the last day, when the Lord says in the Gospel: Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn and weep (Luke 6)?

SALONIUS. In the sacred Scriptures laughter usually signifies joy; hence the Lord in the Gospel: Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh, that is, you will rejoice. And blessed Job says: But the mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter, that is, with joy. So the strong woman, that is, the holy Church, will laugh on the last day, that is, she will rejoice in the recompense of the heavenly kingdom.

VERANUS. Who are the sons of the woman who proclaimed her most blessed? Or who is her husband, who praised her? For he says this: Her sons rose up and proclaimed her most blessed, her sons, and her husband praised her (Prov. 31).

SALONIUS. The sons of this woman, that is, of the holy Church, are all the elect; her husband is the Lord Jesus Christ. For the sons of the Church, namely all the elect, will rise from the dust of the earth on the last day of judgement and, adorned with the glory of immortality, will proclaim their mother most blessed, that is, they will praise the holy Church, which bore them to God from water and the Holy Spirit. Her husband too will rise, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, when on the day of judgement he appears openly in the power of his divinity, and he will praise her, saying in the judgement: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world; I was hungry and you gave me to eat (Matt. 25), and so on.
VERANUS. Why then did he use the past tense, saying: They rose up? For he ought to have said: They will rise.
SALONIUS. What Solomon knew to be future, he held as most certain; and therefore, in the prophetic manner, he used the past for the future.
VERANUS. About whom does he say what follows: Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all (Prov. 31)?
SALONIUS. By many daughters he means the churches of heretics and the crowds of bad catholics.
VERANUS. How are these called daughters of Christ or of the Church? Why are they called children of Christ or of the Church?
SALONIUS. Because of the sacrament of faith and baptism, and the adoption of sons which they received in baptism.
VERANUS. What riches have these daughters gathered?

SALONIUS. Prayers, fasts, alms, affliction and chastity of the flesh, restraint of the tongue, meditation on the Scriptures, and the riches of other good works. These are true riches if they are done with a spiritual intention, namely for the sake of the recompense of the heavenly kingdom; otherwise they profit those who do them nothing. Hence the daughters, namely those of the heretics, or the crowds of bad catholics, have gathered riches for themselves in vain, because either they have erred in faith, or certainly they have not done good works of this kind with a spiritual intention. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works? And then I will declare to them: I never knew you (Matt. 7). But the holy catholic Church has surpassed [them]: that is, she goes beyond all of them, because whatever she does, she does only in right faith and with a spiritual intention.
VERANUS. Of what grace and of what beauty does he speak when he says: Grace is deceitful and beauty vain; the woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised (Prov. 31)?

SALONIUS. Deceitful is the grace of human praise, which hypocrites seek from everyone. Vain beauty is the beauty of chastity or of good works which hypocrites desire to display to men, so that they may be praised by them.
VERANUS. Why is this grace called deceitful and this beauty vain?

SALONIUS. Because it deceives, that is, misleads, pretenders: since while they seek their reward in this life, they will receive no recompense in the future; and if they keep chastity or do any good works, all that they do is vain.
VERANUS. Who is the woman who fears the Lord?
SALONIUS. The holy Church, namely, who in this life always remains in the fear of the Lord, and always desires to fulfil his commands.
VERANUS. How, then, will this woman be praised?
SALONIUS. The same Solomon shows this plainly at the end of this book, when he says: Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates (Prov. 31).
VERANUS. Whose words are these?
SALONIUS. Those of her husband, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
VERANUS. When will he speak these words?

SALONIUS. On the day of judgement, when he commands the angels to lead the Church, after the end of this life, into the joys of the heavenly kingdom. For he will command the angels thus: Give her of the fruit of her hands, that is, of good works. For by hands works are designated; as if he were to say openly: Because she took care to do [the fruit] of good works, that is, love, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, modesty, continence, faith, patience, render to her the reward worthy of this fruit. And let her works praise her in the gates: that is, in the judgement, or at the entrance to the heavenly homeland, let the very works she did praise her; that is, let her be rewarded for the good works she performed.
